d: What Ghost Messaging is, and where to start.
x: Ghost Messaging is one app for the people you talk to: your texts, your friends on Ghost, your circles with their chats, calls and files, and your Telegram, Signal and other chats, side by side. Messages between Ghost apps are sealed end to end, there are no ads, and the app is open source. Ghost Messaging is in alpha It works well enough to use every day, but things still change quickly and some features are marked Coming soon . If you're testing it, start with Join the alpha , and tell us anything odd in the Alpha testers circle. Start here Install the app Android, Mac, Windows or Linux, and what to say yes to. The first time you open it The welcome, and whether Ghost takes over your texts. Your account Create one, keep your recovery words safe, sign in elsewhere. Circles A group with its own spaces: chat, voice, files and texts. The Marketplace Plugins, built in and from other developers. Your texts on a computer Pair the Mac, Windows or Linux app with your phone. Build a plugin Make your own, try it in Developer mode, and submit it. Developer docs How the app is built, both APIs, and a Postman collection. Finding your way around Everything starts from the rail down the left of the screen, the same on every page, as Discord and Slack have. At its head is Messages , your conversations. Under it are your circles , each as its picture: tap one to open it, and a halo in its colour marks the one that's open. A dot beside a circle means something's unread; a red number means someone mentioned you. The circled plus under them starts a new circle or joins one by its link. At the foot: New (start a conversation, a group, a space or a circle), Contacts , Archive , the Marketplace (plugins, as a store) and Settings . Hold a pointer over any of them for its name. Right-click one, or press and hold it on a phone, for its menu: a circle's has its settings and members, Archive's marks everything in it read, and the Marketplace's and Settings' jump to a section. BC NO Messages Codes Circles MC Maya Chen See you at 7! 4:12 2 D Dad 📷 Picture Yesterday BC Book Club Sam: Chapter 9 tonight? Mon The conversations list, with the rail down its left: Messages, your circles, then New, Contacts, Archive, Marketplace and Settings. Prefer a dock? The rail is how you move around the app from 0.9.36. Settings › Developer › Navigation can put back a dock along the foot instead: One dock is the same on every page, and Changing dock is the earlier way, where a circle had a dock of its own. At the top of Messages are three tabs: Messages (texts and chats), Codes (sign-in codes, kept out of the way) and Circles . A few words we use Word What it means Circle A group of people with a sidebar of spaces, a bit like a small server. You can be in as many as you like. Space A room in a circle (or on its own): chat and voice, text only, files, or an SMS space for people without the app. Friend Someone you talk to over Ghost rather than by text: added by their username, or by their number once you've sealed your texts together. Connections Your other chat accounts linked into Ghost: Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, Matrix. Routes How messages travel between Ghost apps: over the relay, or by text. Plugin An extra you add from the Marketplace : for yourself, or, built in, for everyone in a circle. On which devices Android phone : everything, including your texts (SMS and picture messages). Mac, Windows and Linux : friends, circles, calls, files and your other chats on their own, and your texts when paired with your Android phone. iPhone Coming soon : friends, circles and calls. Apple doesn't let apps send or read texts outside the EU, so no texts.

d: Recovery words, your password, the account address, and being the same you on every device.
x: You don't need any of this to use Ghost Messaging. It's here for when you want to know what your account is, where it's kept, and what happens when you sign in somewhere else. One identity, on every device Your account is a key that's yours alone, made from your 12 recovery words. Every device you sign in on becomes that same you: your friends see one person, a circle sees one member, and everything sent to you reaches each of your devices. Your username (like @alex ) is how friends find you. It points at your key. Your password unlocks a sealed backup of your key, so you can sign in with a username and password instead of the words. Your 12 recovery words are the key. They work without the password, and nothing else can replace them. The account address The address that starts with 0x , shown when your account is made and in Settings › Me › Account , is your account's public name. It's the same in any wallet app that takes your 12 words, because it's made from them in the same standard way. Ghost doesn't use it for money; it's simply the one name your account has everywhere. Sharing it is safe; sharing your words is not. What the server keeps The relay server at gogho.st keeps your username and a backup of your key, sealed with your password, which is stretched on your device first. The server can't open it. It never sees your recovery words, your password, or your messages. Kept by the server Never sent to it Your username, and the key it points to Your recovery words Your sealed backup (only your password opens it) Your password Your verified number, if you verify one, to text you codes What you write, to anyone A computer paired with your phone A Mac or PC paired with your phone used to be someone of its own. Now it can be the same you: in Settings › Me › Account on the computer, tap Become the same you as your phone , or sign in to the account your phone is in. Account Become the same you as your phone Keeps who you are now, the same you as your phone Sign in to your Ghost account The account your phone is in On a paired computer. If you lose a device Sign in on another device, with your username and password or your words. In Settings › Me › Account › Signed in on these devices , remove the lost one. It's signed out the next time it connects: a lost iPhone, computer without a phone or browser then deletes everything of your account from itself, and a lost Android phone forgets your recovery words and its keys. If you think someone has your words, make a new account and tell your friends; the words can't be changed.

d: Everyone in a call at about the same loudness.
x: Auto leveler brings everyone in a call to about the same loudness on your device. The friend who always sounds far away comes up, and the one shouting into their microphone comes down, so you stop changing volumes in the middle of a call. Add it: Marketplace › Auto leveler › Add , or turn it on for a whole circle in Circle settings › Plugins . How it works Once someone has talked for a few seconds, Auto leveler knows how loud they arrive and turns them up or down to match everyone else. It moves slowly, so a laugh or a cough doesn't swing anyone, and never more than about 9 dB either way, so a whisper stays a whisper. It changes only what your device plays. Nothing is sent, and nobody else in the call hears anything different. See what it is doing Press and hold someone in the call Their sheet opens with their volume. d: What a plugin of your own can do, what it is made of, and how it reaches the Marketplace.
x: A plugin of your own sorts texts the way you'd like them sorted: bills in a tab of their own with the amount on the row, a parcel's tracking number a press away, receipts marked read as they come. It's one file you write by hand that says what to look for in a text and what to do with it. You try it on your own device in Developer mode, then send it to the Marketplace, where it's reviewed before anyone else can add it. What a plugin can do Tag texts by their words : "your bill is ready", "amount due $45.20", a tracking number. A tag can keep what it found, like the amount. Give texts a tab of their own beside Messages and Codes, or a kind in the list's filter that people show or hide. Draw its texts' rows : a value large on the row (the amount, a tracking number), a short caption, a face with a letter and a colour, and a button at the row's end. Add buttons : lines in a conversation's menu in the list, a button in a conversation's header, lines in a message's menu. A button can say something, copy words to the clipboard, write a reply for you to send, mark the conversation read, move it to one of the plugin's tabs or back to Messages, or open the plugin's own web page. Act as texts come : mark texts in its own tabs and kinds as read, or take their notification away, but only behind a switch in its settings that starts off. Have settings of its own : switches, choices, and words the person types (more words for bills, say), shown on its page in the Marketplace. What it can't do It can't reach the internet, and it isn't code: nothing in it runs. It's a description the app follows. A button you press can open its one web page in your browser, and that's all. It never sees your contacts' texts, group texts, texts sent with Ghost Messaging's encryption, your own messages, chats on other networks (Telegram, Signal and the rest), or circles and spaces. It never acts on a text with a sign-in code in it. It can tag one, but never sort it into a tab, mark it read or silence it. It can't change the words of a message, or who a conversation is from: a row always keeps the conversation's own name. It's for you alone, on one device. Plugins from other developers can't be turned on for a whole circle yet. One file: ghost-plugin/1 A plugin is one file, id .ghostplugin , of JSON in the ghost-plugin/1 format: its name and description, its icon, what it may do, its settings, and its rules. It finds words in a text with phrases like amount due {amount} , never with code or regular expressions, so no plugin can hang the app, and one that's slow is paused. Every field is on The plugin file . { "format": "ghost-plugin/1", "id": "mybills", "version": "1.0.0", "name": "My bills", "tagline": "Bills in a tab of their own", "description": "Texts that say a bill is ready go to a Bills tab, with the amount on the row.", "symbol": "calculator", "hue": "amber", "shelf": "organise", "labels": ["bills"], "permissions": ["sort"], "rules": { "tags": [{"tag": "bill", "any": ["your bill is ready", "amount due {amount}"], "detail": {"from": "token"}}], "sections": [{"key": "bills", "label": "Bills", "icon": "calculator", "kind": "tab", "takes": {"tagged": ["bill"]}, "row": {"value": "{tag:bill}"}}] } } That's a whole plugin, as small as one can be: Developer mode loads it as it is. To submit it, it also needs an icon, your username and a help address ( the whole Bills file has them). Where it runs An Android phone : everything, as your texts come. A computer paired with an Android phone : it sorts the phone's texts there too, once it's added on the computer (plugins are added on each device on its own). Marking read and silencing as texts come happen on the phone only. A Mac or Windows PC on its own has no texts, so a plugin does nothing there. iPhone : plugins from other developers aren't on iPhone at all, because of the App Store's rules for apps that add other developers' features. Developer mode can still load your own there, to try it with Try it . From an idea to the Marketplace Write it Start from one of the examples below and change it, or write one from nothing with The plugin file beside you. Any text editor will do. Try it in Developer mode Load it in Settings › Developer › Plugins in development from a file, a link or the clipboard, then try it on a text without waiting for one to come. Change it, press Reload , try it again. Your first plugin walks through it. Submit it Marketplace › Submit a plugin : the plugin, its icon, description and tags, a screenshot or two, and a note for the reviewer. Submit it to the Marketplace . Review A person at Ghost Messaging reads the whole file, tries it, and approves it, asks for changes or turns it down. Marketplace › My submissions shows where it stands, and the app tells you when that changes. Listed Approved, it's in Discover for everyone with the Reviewed mark, under your username. People see what it can do before they add it, and can report it from its page. The examples Two complete plugins to start from, each one file: Example What it shows Bills An amount found in a text and shown large on its row, a tab and a kind, a setting of the person's own words, and marking receipts read behind a switch. Parcels Words between words, tracking codes, a choice setting, a reply to send, a link, moving a conversation back to Messages, and silencing behind a switch. They're on this site at https://gogho.st/docs/examples/bills.ghostplugin and https://gogho.st/docs/examples/parcels.ghostplugin , which Developer mode can load as they are, and in the app's repository in examples/plugins on GitHub , with a note on each. Their ids, bills and parcels , can't be submitted: give yours an id of its own.

x: A plugin is one file of JSON, named id .ghostplugin , in the ghost-plugin/1 format: one object holding the fields below. It's at most 256 KB (262,144 bytes) and nested at most 8 deep. Numbers in it are whole numbers, and null appears only where a field says it may. A key the format doesn't have is a problem at any depth ( unknown_field ), so a reviewer sees everything a plugin holds. Developer mode loads any file name, and the file laid out however you like. Ids, sections, tags and keys What In the file In the app The plugin id : 3 to 24 lower-case letters and digits, starting with a letter x and its id: Bills is xbills . You'll see it in plugins.list and filters.classify , and its switch is plugin_xbills . No built-in plugin's id starts with x , so yours can never be mixed up with one. A section key : 1 to 12 lower-case letters, no digits x , its id, 0 , its key: xbills0bills . Never other . A tag tag : 1 to 16 lower-case letters and digits, starting with a letter xbills.bill . A plugin's rules read only its own tags: it can't see, give or fake Spam's or Codes'. A setting key : 1 to 24 lower-case letters and digits, starting with a letter Kept as plugin_xbills_extra . An action id : 1 to 24 lower-case letters and digits, starting with a letter Unique within the plugin. A choice value : 1 to 16 lower-case letters and digits Unique within its setting. A pattern broken is bad_key ( bad_id for the plugin's id). These ids are the app's own, and no plugin may have them ( id_reserved ): codes kinds spam embeds actions replies quiet strangers cleaner translate recordcall scribe captions watch debt political sales scams reminders food deliveries appointments notices other ghost ghostmessaging official admin system market marketplace store plugin plugins settings messages , and any id with ghost or gogho in it. The examples' ids, bills and parcels , load in Developer mode like any other, but can't be submitted ( id_example : "That's the example's id: give your plugin an id of its own."), so nobody takes the id every reader of these pages starts with. The icon Not needed in Developer mode: without one, the plugin's tile draws its symbol on its hue. Submitting needs one, and the submission form makes it for you from any picture you choose or paste (256 pixels a side, smaller if it must be), so you only need what follows to put one in the file yourself. A PNG, square, 64 to 512 pixels a side, holding only the chunks IHDR , PLTE , tRNS , sRGB , gAMA , pHYs , IDAT and IEND , with nothing after IEND : so no animation, no text, no EXIF and no colour profile ( bad_icon otherwise). In base64, the standard alphabet with = padding and no spaces or line breaks: at most 48,000 characters, and at most 36,000 bytes once decoded. It's drawn over the plugin's hue, filling its tile. Transparent parts show the hue, so a white glyph on transparency looks like a built-in plugin's tile. To make the base64 on a Mac: base64 -i icon.png | tr -d '\n' In PowerShell on Windows: [Convert]::ToBase64String([IO.File]::ReadAllBytes('icon.png')) Words in a plugin Every string in a plugin, its phrases included, keeps these rules ( bad_text , or phrase_bad_text for a phrase): No space at its start or end. One line. Only the description , whatsNew and settings' hint s may have line breaks, and only the plain one ( \n ). Nothing invisible: no control characters, zero-width spaces or joiners, direction marks or overrides, soft hyphens, private-use characters (one draws a company's logo on some systems), tag characters, or blank-looking letters that make a name look empty. Lengths are counted as JavaScript and Dart count them, in UTF-16 code units: most letters are one, and an emoji is often two. A name, and a section's label, can't be a built-in plugin's or one of their tabs' and kinds', nor have ghost or gogho in it ( name_reserved ). They're compared with look-alikes folded first, so "Сodes" with a Cyrillic С, or "Ｃｏｄｅｓ" in wide letters, is still Codes. Settings Each setting is an object with a type , shown on the plugin's page in the order written; a heading starts a new card. type Fields Shown as toggle key , label (1 to 60), hint (1 to 200), icon , and default ( true or false , required) A switch choice key , label , hint , icon , options (2 to 8 of {"value", "label" (1 to 40), "hint" (1 to 120)} ), and default (one of the values: choice_default otherwise) A choice of one words key , label , hint , icon , placeholder (1 to 60) A field for the person's own words, a line each or with commas between: what a rule does with them note label , hint , icon A line of words heading label , hint A heading over the next card hint , icon and placeholder may be left out; everything else in the table is required. Keys are unique across a plugin's settings ( duplicate ). A rule that names a setting must name one there, of the right kind ( unknown_setting ). A toggle an incoming rule names must start off ( "default": false ), and is switched off again when the plugin is removed. On a computer or an iPhone its hint says it does nothing there. The person's choices are kept when they remove the plugin, and are there again if they add it back. d: Tags, tabs and kinds with their rows, buttons and menu lines, and what happens as texts arrive.
x: A plugin's rules say what it does: tags it gives texts by their words, sections (tabs and kinds) that take tagged texts, actions (buttons and menu lines) and incoming rules for texts as they come. Any of them can say when it applies with a condition. The examples here are from Bills and Parcels . "rules": { "tags": [], // up to 32 tag rules "sections": [], // up to 4 tabs and kinds "actions": [], // up to 12 buttons and menu lines "incoming": [] // up to 8 rules for texts as they come } (JSON has no comments: they're only to say what each is.) Each part may be left out, but a plugin needs at least one tag rule or one section ( empty_pack ). Conditions A condition, a rule's when or a section's takes , is an object whose keys are all optional. Every one given must hold. Key Holds when from The sender is one of these, 1 to 50 of them, each 3 to 64 characters. A number is compared by its digits alone, so +1 (555) 010-0100 and 15550100100 are the same; a name a company texts from is compared in any case. An entry with no digit or letter in it, such as (-) , matches nobody. tagged The text has every one of these tags, 1 to 8 of the plugin's own. untagged It has none of these, 1 to 8. setting A switch's key alone: that switch is on (its default until the person changes it). Or {"key": "level", "is": "loose"} : that choice is loose (its default until changed); for a switch, "is" is "on" or "off" . section Actions only: the conversation is in this section of the plugin's own, or "main" for Messages. Never true in a message's menu, which isn't in a section. Anywhere else it's section_condition . A plugin with an incoming rule can't use from anywhere ( from_with_incoming ): nobody can judge a rule that marks read or silences texts from numbers they don't know. Nor can a plugin with a link button ( bad_link_when ): a tag given by sender, a tab that takes by sender or that tab's row would offer the link for those numbers alone, and pressing it would tell the page which numbers wrote. In a tag rule, tagged and untagged see only the tags given by the rules before it, so naming a tag no earlier rule gives is unknown_tag . Everywhere else, a tag no rule gives is unknown_tag , and a section the plugin doesn't have is unknown_section . There's no condition on groups: a plugin never sees one. Tags A tag rule gives a text a tag when its words match. Several rules may give the same tag: they're different ways to get it. { "tag": "bill", "any": ["your bill is ready", "amount due {amount}"], "atLeast": 1, "none": ["unsubscribe"], "wordsFrom": "extra", "when": {"untagged": ["paid"]}, "detail": {"from": "token"} } Field What it is tag The tag it gives. Required. any 0 to 30 phrases , at least atLeast of which must match. atLeast 1 to 5, and 1 if left out. At most the number of any phrases, unless it has wordsFrom too. all 1 to 8 phrases that must all match. none 1 to 20 phrases none of which may match. wordsFrom A words setting's key: the words the person typed there join any , each a plain phrase ( their own words ). when A condition. detail What the tag keeps: words of your own (1 to 200 characters); {"from": "token"} , what a phrase's first token found; or {"from": "match"} , the whole of what a phrase matched. Nothing if left out. A rule needs something to start it: any , all , wordsFrom , or a when with from or tagged ( tag_rule_no_trigger ). How a text's tags are worked out For each text the plugin sees, its tag rules run in the order they're written, each one like this: If its when doesn't hold, with the tags given so far, the rule is passed over. Its phrases are its any , then the person's words from wordsFrom . If it has either, it counts how many of them match the text; fewer than atLeast , and it's passed over. A rule whose only phrases are the person's words does nothing until they type some. If it has all and one of them doesn't match, or none and one of them does, it's passed over. Its detail: your own words, if that's what it says; for {"from": "token"} , going through its phrases in order, what the first token found in the first phrase that has a token and matches; for {"from": "match"} , the whole match of the first phrase that matches. Trimmed, cut to 200 characters, and nothing where it's empty. The text gets the tag if it hasn't got it yet. If it has it already with no detail, and this rule found one, the detail is kept. Whenever one of the plugin's settings changes, every conversation's tags are worked out again. An example of atLeast {"tag": "school", "any": ["school", "pupils", "uniform", "half term"], "atLeast": 2} "Half term starts Monday: uniform list attached." gets the tag, since two phrases match; "School's out!" doesn't, with one. An example of wordsFrom Bills has a words setting, More words for bills , and its first rule says "wordsFrom": "extra" . Someone who types council tax, water rates there gets "Your council tax is due next week." in their Bills tab, though none of Bills' own phrases match it. Tabs and kinds A section takes the conversations whose last text from them meets its takes . A tab is a tab of its own in the list, beside Messages and Codes; a kind is a line in the list's filter, which people show or hide in Messages as they do the built-in kinds. Field What it is key 1 to 12 lower-case letters, unique in the plugin. label 1 to 24 characters: its tab's words, or its line in the filter. Not a built-in's ( name_reserved ). icon An icon name . kind "tab" or "filter" . leavesMain Tabs only, true if left out: its conversations leave Messages for the tab. false keeps them in Messages too. On a kind it's leaves_main_on_filter . takes A condition with tagged or from ( takes_nothing otherwise), and no section . Required. row How its conversations' rows look ( below ). Every section needs the sort permission. A plugin's kinds start shown, and the person hides one in the filter as they would any kind. Built-in plugins sort first Built-in plugins' tabs and kinds are asked first, then plugins from other developers in the order they were added, each one's sections in the order written: the first that takes a conversation has it. So a plugin never takes what Codes or the spam filter takes, nor what a kind of Kinds of text takes. Kinds of text is on from the start, and its Payment reminders and Deliveries tracking take most bill and parcel texts before any other plugin is asked. Your plugin still tags them, but its tab gets them only where the person switches that kind off, in Marketplace › Kinds of text . Try it says when this happens ("In this app, Kinds of text › Payment reminders takes this text first"), and every plugin's page with tabs or kinds says it to the people who add it: Built-in plugins sort first: a text Codes, Spam filter or a kind of Kinds of text takes stays theirs. Rows A section's row draws its conversations' rows in the list: "row": {"value": "{tag:bill}", "caption": "A bill", "end": "copyamount"} Field What it is value Up to 24 characters, large where the last words would be, with the words small under it. A template . caption Up to 60 characters, a quiet line under the words: why it's in this tab. A template. face {"name": "Parcels", "color": "#4F46E5"} : in place of the sender's face, the first letter of name (1 to 24 characters, plain words) on that colour ( #RRGGBB : bad_color otherwise). end An action's id: its button at the row's end. word An action's id: a word to press after the caption. tap A copy action's id: what tapping the row does, in place of opening the conversation (a long press opens its menu, whose first line is Open conversation ). The row always keeps the conversation's own name. A plugin can't choose what a conversation is called, since anyone who texts could then choose the name their conversation shows. A face's name is plain words with no placeholder, and never a company's logo. The guidelines on other companies' names apply to it. A row's tap can only copy ( verb_not_here ): tapping what looks like a conversation never opens a page or writes anything. An action a row names must list row in its slots ( unknown_action ), and can't be a write ( verb_not_here ). A text with a sign-in code in it never gets a plugin's row. Buttons and menu lines { "id": "copyamount", "label": "Copy the amount", "icon": "copy", "slots": ["row", "list.conversation.menu", "conversation.message.menu"], "when": {"tagged": ["bill"]}, "do": "copy", "text": "{tag:bill}", "say": "Amount copied" } An action has an id , a label (1 to 32 characters), an icon , 1 to 4 different slots , an optional when , what it does ( do ), and that verb's fields. Slot Where it shows row On its sections' rows, where a row's end , word or tap names it. list.conversation.menu A line in a conversation's menu in the list (a long press). At most 3 actions ( slot_full ). conversation.header A button in a texts conversation's header. At most 1 ( header_full ). conversation.message.menu A line in a message's menu in a texts conversation. At most 3. do Its fields Needs Slots What it does say text (1 to 80) nothing every one Shows those words for a moment. copy text (a template, 1 to 200), say (1 to 80, Copied if left out) copy every one Copies the text to the clipboard, and says so. write text (1 to 300) write conversation.header , conversation.message.menu Writes the text in the conversation's box, for the person to send or not. markread none markread every one Marks that conversation read. move to : "main" , or one of its own tabs' keys move row , list.conversation.menu , conversation.header Moves that conversation to the tab, or back to Messages. link url : the plugin's one links address links every one Opens that page in the browser. Only a copy's text holds placeholders. A label, a say 's text, a copy's say and a write 's text have no { or } at all ( bad_template ): a stranger's words never reach the app's menus, and the words a button writes are the words the reviewer read. A move goes only to Messages or one of the plugin's own tabs, never to a kind ( verb_not_here ). A link opens only the plugin's one address ( link_not_declared ), and a plugin with one can't use from anywhere, so which texts offer the button can't tell a server which numbers wrote. An action is offered only where its when holds and the plugin sees the text, and a copy only where its placeholders can be filled. Its section condition reads the section the conversation is in. The list's menu, a texts conversation's header and its messages' menu are where they show. Telegram, Signal and spaces' chats never show a plugin's buttons. A plugin's buttons are kept from running away: words it says are shown at most once every second and a half, and it can copy at most ten times a minute. As texts arrive {"in": "receipts", "do": ["markread"], "setting": "autoread"} An incoming rule marks a text read, or takes its notification away, as it comes: in is one of the plugin's own sections, do is markread , mute or both, setting is the switch that turns it on, and when is an optional condition. It acts when the conversation is in that section, the switch is on and the condition holds. The switch must start off ( "default": false : incoming_needs_toggle ), so nothing is marked read or silenced until the person switches it on. It runs on the phone, while the app is open, after Android has shown the notification, which it then takes away: the sound has played by then. Nothing runs while the app is closed. It never runs on a computer, nor on a paired iPhone. Its switch's hint says so there. mute is for one text at a time: it takes away that text's notification and never mutes the conversation, so the next text there notifies as usual unless it too is in that section with the switch on. markread marks the conversation read, which takes its notification away too. d: How a plugin finds words in a text: phrases, tokens like {digits:6}, and what a match gives it.
x: A plugin finds words in a text with phrases : plain words, like your bill is ready , with tokens where something varies, like amount due {amount} . There are no regular expressions and no code. The app turns each phrase into a search of its own making, with every repeat in it bounded, so a phrase can't run away with a phone however long or strange the text it reads. A phrase A phrase is 1 to 120 characters on one line, keeping the rules for words in a plugin . Read from left to right: { starts a token , which runs to the next } : a name, then optionally :N or :N-M . {digits:6} is {digits:6-6} , exactly six digits. {{ is a plain { , and }} a plain } . A run of spaces is one gap, which matches any run of space in the text: one space, several, a line break. Everything else is matched as it is: letters in any case, and every other character as itself. A . is a full stop, never "any character". The tokens Token Matches For example {digits:N-M} A run of N to M digits, not part of a longer run. 1 to 24, and 1-24 if you give no numbers. your code is {digits:4-8} finds 123456 in "Your code is 123456.", and nothing in "Your code is 1234567890". {number} A number: 1,234, 1.234,5, 98765 or 12.5. The whole run of digits, dots and commas it sits on, or nothing: 192.168.1.1 is no number. order {number} finds 1,234 in "Order 1,234 shipped". {amount} A number with a currency sign or code before or after it: $45.20, 45,00 EUR, £30. The signs are $, €, £, ¥ and ₹; the codes USD, EUR, GBP, CAD and AUD, in any case. amount due {amount} finds $1,234.56 in "Amount due $1,234.56 by Friday", and nothing in "Amount due 45 by Friday". {code:N-M} A whole word of N to M letters and digits with at least one digit in it. 4 to 24, and 4-10 if you give no numbers. code {code:4-8} finds AB12CD in "Use code AB12CD to sign in", and nothing in "Use code ABCDEF to sign in". {word} One word: letters, digits, ' and - . {word} delivery finds Acme in "Your Acme delivery is near". {words:N-M} N to M words of anything but spaces, between two plain parts of the phrase. 0 to 4, and 1-3 if you give no numbers. your {words:0-3} has shipped finds "new blue parcel" in "Your new blue parcel has shipped!" {url} A web address starting http:// , https:// or www. . track {url} finds https://example.com/t/123 in "track https://example.com/t/123 now". {email} An email address. from {email} finds bob.smith+x@mail.example.co.uk in "Reply from bob.smith+x@mail.example.co.uk." {phone} A phone number of 7 to 15 digits, with spaces, brackets, dots or dashes among them. The whole run it sits on, or nothing: two numbers with only a space between them read as one run. {phone} finds +1 (555) 010-0100 in "Call +1 (555) 010-0100 today". {date} A date: 12/03/2026, 2026-11-20, March 5th, 5 jan. Months are in English. on {date} finds March 5th in "Your appointment on March 5th at 3pm". {time} A time: 3pm, 10:30 a.m., 14:05. at {time} finds 10:30 a.m. in "See you at 10:30 a.m. sharp". The rules a phrase keeps A phrase that breaks one of these doesn't load, and says which at its place in the file ( rules.tags[0].any[2] ). They're checked in this order, and the first one broken is the problem given. Rule Broken by Problem Two tokens need something between them. {digits:4}{digits:4} phrase_tokens_touch A token can't touch a letter or digit. Punctuation may touch one: #{digits:4-10} and code:{code} are fine. bill{digits:4} phrase_token_touches_word {words} needs a space on each side, so it can't be first or last. {words:1-2} bill phrase_words_edge {url} must be followed by a space or the end of the phrase. {url}. phrase_url_followed At most 4 tokens, and only one {words} and one {url} among them. a {digits} b {digits} c {digits} d {digits} e {digits} phrase_too_many_tokens A phrase with no token needs at least two letters or digits. a phrase_too_short Besides those: a token the app doesn't know, numbers it can't take, a { with no } or a } on its own is phrase_bad_token ( {digits:0} , {digits:9-4} , {foo} , code {code:3} , go {words:5} , x {word:2} y , bill } ). An empty phrase, one over 120 characters, one with a space at its start or end, a line break or an invisible character is phrase_bad_text . How a phrase matches Whole words. A phrase that starts or ends with a letter or digit matches only whole words there: bill finds "bill" in "Your bill is ready", but nothing in "Your billing statement". Any case. Letters match in either case, accented ones too: your appt finds "YOUR APPT", and café finds "CAFÉ". Curly quotes and dashes. Before matching, the text and the phrase both have curly quotes made straight, dashes made - and odd spaces made plain ones, so don't forget finds "Don’t forget" written with a curly apostrophe. The first 2,000 characters of a text are read, and the rest isn't. The anchor. A phrase's longest run of plain letters and digits (a to z, 0 to 9), at least three long, is its anchor: the first, where two are as long. The phrase is only tried on a text that has its anchor in it, in any case, which is how hundreds of phrases stay quick. your code is {digits:4-8} 's anchor is your , and tracking no. {code:8-24} 's is tracking . A phrase with no such run, like {phone} , at {time} or café , is anchorless : it's tried on every text, so a plugin may have only 8. What a match gives A match gives two things: the whole of what the phrase matched, and what its first token found. A tag rule's detail keeps one of them for its tag, for a row or a copy button to show: {"from": "token"} : what the first token found. amount due: {amount} on "Amount due: 45,00 EUR." keeps 45,00 EUR. {"from": "match"} : the whole match. The same phrase keeps "Amount due: 45,00 EUR". Each is trimmed, and an empty one keeps nothing: your {words:0-3} has shipped matches "Your has shipped", with no detail. So a slow plugin is caught, and a phone that was only busy for a moment isn't held against it. More than 100 milliseconds of reading in any one second is a strike too, where its texts took it a millisecond or more each on average. The app reads every conversation again whenever a switch or a setting changes, and a plugin that's quick on each text isn't held against that. More than half of any one second spent reading is a strike however quick it is on each text, so a plugin that's nearly a millisecond a text can't hold the app for seconds every time a switch changes. The first text after it starts never counts: that's when its phrases are made ready. Five strikes in ten minutes pause it. It does nothing while paused, its page says Paused: it was slowing the app down. with Turn it back on , and the pause is kept, across restarts, until then or a new version. The person's own words A words setting lets the person type words of their own, a line each or with commas between. A tag rule's wordsFrom names that setting, and each of the first 50 entries, cut to 60 characters, becomes a phrase that joins the rule's any . d: Permissions, what each one lets a plugin do, and what people are told before they add it.
x: A plugin's permissions list what it may do beyond reading texts to tag them. Each one a rule uses must be listed ( needs_permission ), and each one listed must be used ( permission_unused ), so the list is always exactly what the plugin does. People see it before they add a plugin, and on its page under What it reads and keeps , in lines the app makes from the file itself: never from the developer's own words, and never from anything the Marketplace's server says. The permissions, and what people see Permission Needed for The line people see (always) Reads texts from numbers not in your contacts : Their words and who they're from, on this phone, to sort them. Never your contacts' texts, group texts, texts sent with Ghost Messaging's encryption, your own, chats on other networks, or circles and spaces. Nothing at all while Ghost Messaging can't read your contacts. sort any tab or kind Sorts texts into its own tabs and kinds : They leave Messages for its tab while it's added. Remove it and they're back. Texts with a sign-in code in them are never sorted. move a move button Moves a conversation when you ask : Only when you press its button, into its own tabs or back to Messages. markread a markread button, or an incoming rule that marks read Can mark texts as read : Only the conversation you press it on, or texts in its own tabs and kinds as they come once you switch that on in its settings. A text marked read loses its notification. mute an incoming rule that silences Can silence notifications : Only texts in its own tabs and kinds, once you switch that on in its settings. Each one's notification is taken away as it comes. copy a copy button Copies to your clipboard when you ask : Only when you press its button. write a write button Writes a reply for you to send : Only when you press its button. Nothing is sent until you send it. links a link button Opens example.com in your browser , with its link's own host: Only when you press its button. The address never changes, and nothing from your texts goes with it. (always) Can't reach the internet : It has no way to send anything over the internet itself. A button you press can open its page in your browser or copy words to your clipboard. They're shown in that order. "This phone" is the device it's on: on a computer the first line says "on this computer", and on an iPhone "on this iPhone". On a computer or an iPhone Incoming rules run only on the phone, so on a computer or an iPhone the lines say less: The Can silence notifications line is left out. Can mark texts as read is there only for a markread button, with the hint "Only the conversation you press it on." In what it adds, the lines for incoming rules become one: "On your phone it can also mark read or silence texts as they come; not on this computer." (or "not on this iPhone.") What it adds Under the lines above, the sheet and the plugin's page say what it adds, made from its rules in this order: each tab: "A Bills tab in the list"; each kind: "A kind in the list's filter: Receipts"; "Choices in a conversation's menu in the list", "A button in a conversation's header" and "Choices in a message's menu", each once where a button is there; on a phone, each incoming rule: "Can mark Receipts texts as read as they come, once you switch it on", or "Can silence Parcels texts as they come, once you switch it on"; "Settings of its own, on its page", where it has settings. x: Developer mode loads a plugin you're making straight onto your own device, unreviewed, so you can try it, change it and load it again before anyone else sees it. Plugins in development load only in Developer mode, and run only while it's on: switch it off and they stop, switch it back on and they're there again. While one is on, the list of conversations says so in a quiet line: A plugin in development is on · Settings › Developer . They show in the Marketplace too, under Marketplace › In development and as In development · not reviewed on their pages, so one never looks like a reviewed plugin. d: What gets a plugin listed, what keeps one out, and how reports and withdrawals work.
x: Plugins in the Marketplace read people's texts, so they're held to more than working. These are what review looks for. Sending a plugin means saying, in the form, "I made this plugin, and it follows the Marketplace guidelines". What gets a plugin listed It does what it says. Its name, short line and description say what it does, and it does that and nothing else. Its phrases are precise. They match the texts it's for and not others. A phrase that's one short word, or a word like "your", catches far too much: Try the samples shows what yours catches, and a dinner plan or a sign-in code should come out untouched. What marks texts read or silences them is behind a setting , off until the person switches it on. The file format makes sure of that, so it's only a matter of saying clearly, in the setting's words, what it does. Its help link or email works , and reaches you. Its screenshots show it as it is , with made-up texts. Its words are plain. A description that says what it does, with no web addresses in it and no promises it can't keep. What keeps one out Another company's name, logo or marks anywhere in a plugin: its name, short line, description, tabs and kinds, faces, buttons, settings, icon or screenshots; or in your username or help address. A plugin that sorts a bank's texts can say "bank", not the bank's name. Looking like Ghost Messaging or a built-in plugin : its name, icon, colours or words. Screenshots showing real people's messages, names or numbers , yours included. Links to anything but your own pages. A plugin's one link is for its help or its own site. Anything hateful, sexual or harassing , in any of its words or pictures. Replies that aren't plain and polite. A button that writes a reply writes words the person sends as their own. Reports Anyone who has a plugin, or sees it in the Marketplace, can report it from its page with Report this plugin : why (it's misleading; it's harmful or abusive; it's spam; it asks too much of their texts; it doesn't work; or something else) and a few words. Their username goes with it only if they switch on Send my username with it . Every report is read, by a person, as soon as we can, and the harmful ones first. A report can lead to a plugin being taken off the Marketplace, a version being withdrawn, or its developer being blocked. Unlisting, withdrawing and blocking Unlisting takes a plugin off the Marketplace: nobody new can add it, and people who have it keep it. You can do it yourself from My submissions; review can do it too, and then only review can list it again. Withdrawing is for a version that should never have been approved. Every device that has it switches it off and says so ("Trips was withdrawn from the Marketplace and is off."), and its page gives the reviewer's reason: "Withdrawn from the Marketplace: … It's off, and does nothing until you remove it." It offers only Remove , and Update where a newer version is approved. The developer sees Withdrawn by review , with the same reason. An approved update doesn't withdraw the version before it unless review chooses to, so nobody's plugin stops working because they haven't updated yet. Blocking a developer stops them submitting ("This account can't submit plugins."), and may take their plugins off the Marketplace too.

d: What is sealed, what the server sees, blocking, reporting, and signing out.
x: Ghost Messaging is built so the people running its server can't read what you say. There are no ads, and the app is open source, so anyone can check. What's sealed end to end What Sealed end to end? Messages between friends, and in groups of friends Yes, with forward secrecy Circles and spaces: chat, files, polls Yes, with a key the circle's members share Calls Yes, between the people in them: through Ghost's relay, or directly where the relay can't be reached, still sealed Your texts with one person, with encryption on Yes Ordinary texts and picture messages No: they go through your carrier, as all texts do Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp and Matrix chats As those networks seal them; they go between your device and the network, not through Ghost What the server sees Which installs talk to each other, and when, as any server passing messages would. Your username, and your account backup sealed with your password (which it never sees). Your verified number, if you verify one, to text you codes. It's shown to nobody unless you choose. Never: what you write, your files, your recovery words or your password. On your device Spam filtering, sorting, translation, summaries, captions and transcripts all happen on your device. Your texts stay in your phone's own store. Plugins say on their pages what they can see. Plugins from other developers are reviewed before they're listed. They never see your contacts' texts, group texts, encrypted texts or your own (and nothing at all while Ghost Messaging can't read your contacts, since it couldn't tell them from strangers), and they have no way to send anything over the internet: a button you press can open the plugin's page in your browser or copy words to your clipboard. The Marketplace is fetched from our server, which sees your device's address and which plugins you add, and keeps no record of either. A report sends the plugin, what you chose and wrote, and your username only if you say so. A plugin you submit is listed with your username, help address and screenshots. Blocking and archiving Block someone from a conversation's menu or their card; a Ghost person when you report them. Settings › Blocked lists everyone you've blocked, Telegram and Signal people too, and unblocks them. Archive a conversation by swiping it left. Settings › Archived (or Archive in the rail) has them; a new message brings one back. Forward secrecy Messages between friends, and the copies your devices send each other, are sealed so that they stay safe even if your recovery words, your password or your account backup leak later. Each of your devices makes a fresh key every day and deletes it about two weeks later. A message is sealed with a one-off key that is thrown away as soon as it's sent. Someone who saved the scrambled traffic can't open it afterwards, even with your recovery words. What it doesn't cover: the messages saved on your devices (whoever has your unlocked phone can read your history), who you talk to and when, and data texts. It also doesn't cover circles yet, or messages to someone who has a device on an older version of Ghost; those use the earlier sealing. If your recovery words leak, someone could pretend to be you from then on. Compare safety numbers if something seems off, and make a new account if your words were exposed. Reporting Report someone who sends spam, harasses you, pretends to be someone else or shares something illegal. Ghost doesn't scan anyone's messages: a report is how the team hears about it. A message: press and hold it in a chat with a friend, a group of friends, or a space, and choose Report . A person: open their card (tap their name or picture) and choose Report . Choose why, add a note if you like, and press Send report . Reporting a person also offers to block them: you stop being friends, and their friend requests and messages to you are dropped. Unblock them in Settings › Blocked . Our server can't read your chats, so a message report takes the message and up to five messages either side of it with it, because you choose to hand them over. The report is sealed on your device so that only the Ghost Messaging reviewer can open it: the server keeps it without being able to read it. Your username goes with it, so the reviewer can tell reports apart; the person you report isn't told who reported them. Settings › Reports you've made lists what you've reported from this device: who, why and when, never the messages. In circles A circle's messages are sealed with a key everyone in it has. Forward secrecy doesn't cover circles yet. Removing someone stops their app joining, but it doesn't change that key, so an old or altered app that kept it could still read what's said. For anything a removed person mustn't read, make a new circle. See Removing someone . Leaving Settings › Me › Remove everything about me unlinks every account and your number, and clears your watch list, on the phone and on the server. Settings › Me › Account › Sign out of this device signs the device out. On an iPhone or a computer without a phone it offers to delete everything of your account from it too, and a browser always does; an Android phone, or a computer linked to one, keeps its texts and conversations. Doesn't yet: calls, circles and spaces (each is a room on one relay), and who's online. The app says so instead of ringing a friend on another relay, keeps their ring as a missed call, and leaves them out of circles and spaces. Kept on each relay apart: usernames ( @maya on yours and @maya@relay.example can be two people), your account and its backup, invite words and Files spaces. Add-me links look the name up on the relay you use, so on a relay of your own they may find someone else, or nobody. The app warns you before it sends a request. Still works with anyone: texts (SMS), including encrypted ones. The Marketplace always comes from gogho.st. Off on a relay of your own unless you set them up: calls through a TURN server, verifying numbers by text, linking Discord, X or Telegram. Closed iPhones can't be woken by your relay. Someone on an older version of the app can't be reached from another relay: the app tells you they need a newer one. Where it is their relay that doesn't pass messages on, it says that instead. So a relay of your own suits a group that moves together, for its circles, spaces and calls, and its people can still be friends with people elsewhere. How to run one (Docker, or systemd behind Caddy or nginx, with coturn for calls) is in the repository: docs/SELF_HOSTING.md , with sample files in relay/deploy/ . Direct Coming soon A second way between Ghost apps, tried after the relay server: straight from one device to another, with no server in between. The relay stays first, because it is fast and keeps a message for someone who is away. The direct route is the way through when the relay can't carry something, for instance when it can't be reached. Your device links only with your own other devices and with your friends' devices. They are told where it is in sealed messages; nobody else is, and nothing is put in any public directory. What crosses a direct link is sealed exactly as it is through the relay. Routes Routes Relay server Through a server on the internet. The server sees who talks to whom, never what is said. Direct Straight between your devices and your friends', with no server in between. Their device sees your network address; nobody else does. SMS As data texts over the phone network. Each counts as a text on your plan. The ways this phone reaches another, tried from the top. Direct Knows 3 friends' devices And 1 other device of your own. Linked to 1 device now 1 straight. Only through link helpers Friends' devices then see the link helper's address and not this device's. It is slower. A link helper sees which devices link and how much they send, never who they are or what is said. Settings › Routes, in a build that has the direct route. Who counts as a friend: only someone you and they both said yes to, as a friend by username or by number. People you share a group with, and people who have only asked, are never linked with or told anything. What a friend's device learns: your device's network address, as with any direct connection, and on a phone only while you're using the app. Switch on Only through link helpers and friends are told at once, and from then see the helper's address instead; links are slower then. It is off unless you switch it on, because where the relay names no link helper, nothing would link at all. Link helpers are servers that help two devices find each other across networks, and pass their sealed packets along where no straight path can be made. The relay you use names them. Where it names none, direct links work only between devices on the same network. On a phone the direct network runs only for something of your own: a message you send, or the relay being unreachable while you use the app. It stops two minutes after, whatever a friend's device does, so it doesn't wear the battery down. On a computer it stays up while the route is on. Invisible: while you've chosen to be shown as Invisible, your device makes no direct links with friends' devices, since a link would show it is there. Your own devices still link with each other. Off: switch Direct off under Routes and nothing is linked, and nobody is told where your device is. If it can't start on your device, Settings › Routes says why under Direct , and every other route works as before. How the relay is checked The relay is fast and keeps messages for people who are away, so it comes first. Your app also checks what it says, so a relay that drops something, keeps it back, or gives someone's username to another key doesn't go unnoticed. Usernames. Each friend you added by username is looked up again once a day, and your own each time you connect. If the relay that once gave a friend's username to them now gives it to another account, their profile says so; usually it's because they changed or gave up their username and someone else took it. Either way you're still talking to the friend you added: the relay can't swap them for someone else. If a friend tells their app they go by a new username, and the relay agrees, that's the one looked up from then on. Their app is told too, through the relay and over a direct link where one is open. Each relay is its own directory, so on a relay of your own nobody's username is held against what ours said. If you use Ghost Messaging on several devices, they take turns: your friends are still looked up once a day between them, and each of your devices shows what was found. These lookups and the checks on friend requests use at most a quarter of what the relay answers your account in an hour, leaving the rest for adding friends and accepting requests. If the relay ever says that's used up, Accept tells you by when it frees up. Your own username. If the relay gives it to another account, you're told once, calmly, with the usual reasons: you gave it up or changed it on another of your devices, made a new key for this phone (the old key still holds it), or use another relay. Add-me links carry your account's name (made from your key) after a # , which no browser sends to any server. Whoever opens your link adds that key and no other, whatever the relay says. Messages Coming soon . With Direct , your device and a friend's compare, over a direct link, which messages went between them and when, never what they said. Anything your device never got is sent again straight. Only once it has come is anything held against the relay, and then as the friend's device's word. A device that was away while another of yours took a message, or a message lost when the relay restarted, isn't counted against it. Check now dials the friends the relay says are online, once a minute at most; with no direct link in use, a few are checked by themselves while the app is open. SMS as a route When the relay can't be reached, a message to a friend can go as a data text over the phone network instead: still sealed, needing no internet, and reaching a phone whose app is closed. Each one counts as a text on your plan, so only small messages go this way. d: The major parts of Ghost Messaging, where each lives in the source, and what it talks to.
x: Ghost Messaging is one Flutter app for Android, iPhone, Mac, Windows and Linux, a small relay server, and a few helper programs. This page is a map of the source for someone about to read or change it: what each part is for, where it lives, and what it talks to. Paths are from the repository's root ( github.com/InfamousVague/ghost-messaging ). Screens lib/ui, lib/kit, packages/glacier Texts lib/sms.dart People lib/friends, lib/me, lib/account Circles, spaces, calls lib/circles, lib/voice, lib/files Other networks lib/inbox Plugins lib/plugins, lib/market Whoever answers the screens Android itself, a paired phone, or the app alone Routes lib/net: the switchboard, the hub route, the SMS route Native code android/, ios/, macos/, windows/, linux/, native/voicefx Relay server relay/: hub, pairing, files, Marketplace Helper programs sidecar/, discord/ Where things are Folder What it holds lib/ The app, in Dart, for every platform. android/ The Android half, in Kotlin: SMS and MMS, notifications, encryption keys, the link to paired computers, the Google Messages bridge, the updater. ios/ , macos/ , windows/ , linux/ Each platform's runner, with the native pieces the app calls: call recording, captions, transcripts, sounds, updates, deep links. native/voicefx The microphone's noise removal and gain, in C (RNNoise, and DeepFilterNet where built in), shared by every platform. packages/glacier Glacier, the UI kit the screens are drawn with. A copy; it is changed in its own repository. relay/ The relay server: a Dart program with no dependencies beyond Dart's own library. sidecar/ Four Go programs the app runs beside itself, one each for Google Messages, Signal, WhatsApp and Matrix. discord/ A Node program: the bot that shows a Discord server's voice channels and bridges one into a space. tool/ Build, release and deploy scripts, asset generators, and tests that run against a live relay. site/ , docs-src/ gogho.st and these docs. docs-src is the source; tool/build-docs.mjs writes site/docs . docs/ Maintainers' notes, one per large feature: the network, the desktop link, friends, groups, the Marketplace. examples/plugins Example plugins in the ghost-plugin/1 format. test/ , integration_test/ The app's tests, and the pictures its screen tests are held to ( test/shots ). One app, several ways of running Every screen asks for what it needs through one object, Sms.instance ( lib/sms.dart ): the conversations, a thread's messages, sending, the settings. Sms passes each call by name to whatever is set as Sms.calls , and which object that is decides how the app runs . The screens are the same in every case. Answered by Where Used when The platform channel ghost_messaging/sms lib/sms.dart , android/…/MainActivity.kt An Android phone. Kotlin reads and writes Android's own SMS and MMS database. OverlayCalls lib/standalone/overlay.dart Android, wrapped round the channel: conversations with @username friends are answered in Dart, the rest passed on. StandaloneCalls lib/standalone/standalone.dart An iPhone, or a computer with no phone linked: the app's own network and nothing from a phone. LinkCalls lib/desktop/remote.dart A computer paired with an Android phone: each call becomes a sealed request to the phone. DeskOwnCalls lib/desktop/own_calls.dart A paired computer the phone has handed its identity to: friends and circles run on the computer itself, texts still come from the phone. lib/main.dart chooses: a computer goes to desktopMain() ( lib/desktop/main.dart ), an iPhone starts on its own, and Android starts on the channel. From there both paths load the person's choices ( AppState , lib/app_state.dart ), the plugins, the API, and then the network through startPeople ( lib/people.dart ), which starts the routes, friends, groups, spaces and circles in that order. Texts on Android The app keeps no copy of your texts: they live in Android's SMS and MMS database, which is why changing texting apps loses nothing. The Kotlin side is in android/app/src/main/kotlin/com/infamousvague/ghostmessaging . File What it does MainActivity.kt Answers the channel's calls and sends events back ( ghost_messaging/events ): a conversation changed, something to open. Store.kt Reads and writes Android's database: the list, threads, messages, contacts. Messaging.kt Sending ( Sender ) and the receivers for texts arriving, MMS arriving, and sent and delivered reports. Pdu.kt The MMS wire format, written and read by hand. Notifier.kt Notifications, with Reply and Mark as read. E2e.kt , E2eCrypto.kt Encrypted texts with one person, and the phone's key pair, held under the Android Keystore. GmBridge.kt , GmWeb.kt Running beside Google Messages : reading its notifications, or its web connection through sidecar/gmessages . Desk.kt , DeskSession.kt , DeskCrypto.kt , DeskService.kt The phone's half of the link to paired computers . Routes: how apps reach each other Everything between two Ghost apps (a friend's message, a call's setup, a space's chat) goes through lib/net . Its idea is the route : one way of getting bytes to another install, behind an interface ( Carrier , lib/net/carrier.dart ) so a new one can be added without the app above knowing. Part Where What it does Envelope and packet lib/net/packet.dart An envelope is a small JSON message with a kind ( text , call , room , hello …). A packet is an envelope as a route carries it: a version byte, the sender's 16-byte name, then the envelope, sealed. Long ones cross a short route in parts. The switchboard lib/net/switchboard.dart Chooses a route for each thing sent, falls back to the next, seals and opens, joins parts, drops second copies, and answers what asks for an answer. The hub route lib/net/hub_carrier.dart A WebSocket to the relay server's hub. Also where presence and rooms come from. Its protocol . The SMS route lib/net/sms_carrier.dart , android/…/NetSms.kt Packets as data texts: 133 bytes each, six at most, costing a text each, and able to wake a closed app. Keys and sealing lib/net/crypto.dart , android/…/Net.kt P-256 key agreement, HKDF-SHA256 and AES-256-GCM. Kotlin and Dart are held to the same bytes by tests on both sides. The app's hold on it all lib/net/net.dart Net : starts the routes, knows who can be reached, and is what the rest of the app sends through. The routes are tried in the person's order ( Settings › Routes ). One is passed over when it is off, down, can't reach that person, can't hold the packet, or costs money and the message isn't one allowed to. Only the hub and SMS routes exist today; the interface leaves room for a local-network and a peer-to-peer one. Who someone is An install is a P-256 key pair. Its name everywhere on the network is the first 16 bytes of the SHA-256 of its public key, in hex. The relay knows installs by that name and nothing else. An account ( lib/account ) is twelve recovery words. From them come an address that names the account, and the keys that seal its backup, which is kept on the relay sealed twice: once under the password, once under the words. How your account works is the plain account of it. A profile ( lib/me/me.dart ): the username, linked handles and verified number, kept by the relay's directory as hashes. Friends : by number ( lib/friends/friends.dart , for people encryption is on with) and by username ( lib/friends/buddies.dart ). Groups of friends are lib/friends/groups.dart : each message goes to each member by the routes. Circles, spaces and calls A space (in the code, a hangout or voice channel) is 32 random bytes, its seed. The room's name on the hub, the token that lets someone in and the key everything in it is sealed with are all made from the seed ( VoiceChannel , lib/voice/voice.dart ), so whoever holds a space's link holds all three and the relay holds none. lib/voice/channels.dart ( Voice ): the spaces someone is in, and making, sharing, joining and leaving them. lib/voice/hangout.dart ( HangoutRoom ): a space's chat. History is passed between members; the hub only holds packets for whoever is away. lib/voice/rtc.dart : the call itself, WebRTC from each member to each other. Offers, answers and candidates are sealed with the space's key and said in its room; sound and picture never go through the relay's hub. lib/voice/roles.dart : a space's roles, as a numbered list signed by its owner. lib/circles : a circle is one seed and a signed manifest listing its spaces, roles and settings ( CircleManifest , lib/circles/circle.dart ). Members pass the newest manifest to each other. lib/files : a Files space . Files are sealed on the device in 256 KiB pieces ( lib/net/file_seal.dart ) and kept by the relay, which sees sizes and never names or contents. Other networks lib/inbox puts other services' chats in the same list. Each is an InboxNetwork ( lib/inbox/inbox.dart ) with its own way of connecting: Network How Telegram TDLib, loaded into the app ( lib/inbox/td_json.dart ). Signal, WhatsApp, Matrix A helper program each ( sidecar/ ), started by the app and spoken to in lines of JSON over its input and output. Each helper's PROTOCOL.md says what is said. Google Chat, Microsoft Teams Their own web APIs, straight from the app. Nothing from these networks goes through Ghost's relay. Paired computers A computer paired with a phone shows the phone's texts by asking the phone for them. The computer's half is lib/desktop/link ( PhoneLink , LinkSession ); the phone's is DeskSession.kt . They connect over the local network where they can and through the relay's pairing channel where they can't, and either way every frame is sealed with keys made from the pairing, so the relay passes bytes it can't read. What the computer has read is kept sealed on its disk ( lib/desktop/cache.dart ). Plugins and the Marketplace A plugin adds to the conversations list and to texts through a few fixed points ( lib/plugins/plugin.dart ): tagging a message, a section or tab in the list, a button, a rule for what arrives. The built-in ones are Dart classes ( lib/plugins/registry.dart ). One from another developer is data, never code : a JSON file ( lib/plugins/pack ) the app reads into those same points, held to what it declared by GatedHost . The Marketplace ( lib/market , and relay/lib/market.dart on the server) lists reviewed plugins. An approval is a reviewer's signature over the plugin's id, version and its file's SHA-256, checked against keys the app ships with, at install and at every start: the server can withhold a plugin but can't make one look reviewed. The relay server relay/bin/relay.dart starts one HTTP server; relay/lib/relay.dart sends each request to its part. Part File What it does Pairing channels relay.dart Passes sealed frames between a phone and its computer while both are connected. Keeps no frame. The hub hub.dart Where installs find each other: signing in with a key, packets passed or held for whoever is away, presence, rooms. The directory handles.dart , accounts.dart , invites.dart , invite_words.dart Usernames, linked handles, number verification, sealed account backups, invitations and circles' invite words. Reached through the hub's connection. Files files.dart , files_roster.dart Files spaces' sealed pieces and their log. Marketplace market.dart , market_pack.dart , market_store.dart Plugins' submissions, review and listing. Pushes, feedback pushes.dart , feedback.dart A "New message" push to an iPhone something is held for; feedback sent from the app. Arithmetic p256.dart , secp256k1.dart , sha256.dart , keccak.dart Signature checking and hashes, written out so the relay depends on nothing. What it can see is the same throughout: which installs talk, when, and how much. Its HTTP routes and its WebSocket protocols are documented in full. Screens lib/ui/shell.dart ( AppShell ) is the frame: the list and what is open beside it, side by side where the window is wide. lib/ui/conversations.dart is the list, lib/ui/thread.dart a conversation, lib/ui/hangout_screen.dart a space, lib/ui/voice_screen.d

d: Five things followed from the tap to the wire: a text, a message to a friend, a call, pairing a computer, and adding a plugin.
x: The quickest way into the source is to follow one thing through it. Here are five, each from the tap to the wire, naming the file at every step. How the app is built says what each part is. Sending a text On an Android phone where Ghost Messaging is the texting app. The box decides lib/ui/thread.dart : words alone to one friend go by the routes (the next section). Anything else is a text: Sms.instance.send . Dart to Kotlin lib/sms.dart passes send to Sms.calls . On Android that is the overlay ( lib/standalone/overlay.dart ), which passes a phone number on to the channel ghost_messaging/sms , answered in MainActivity.kt . Sender chooses SMS or MMS Sender.send in Messaging.kt . One person and no attachment is an SMS, sealed first by E2e.kt where encryption is on with them. Several people, or a picture, is an MMS, which Pdu.kt encodes. Android's database, then the radio Store.kt writes the message to Android's own database, and Android's SmsManager sends it. Reports of sent and delivered come back to SmsStatusReceiver . The screen hears Bus.changed sends an event up ghost_messaging/events ; Sms.instance.changes fires and the thread and list read again. A text arriving runs the other way: SmsDeliverReceiver in Messaging.kt writes it, Notifier.kt shows it, paired computers are told, and the screen hears the same event. A message to a friend Kept first Friends.sendText ( lib/friends/friends.dart ) stores the message where the person's texts are, so it is in the conversation whether or not it has gone. Into an envelope An Envelope of kind text goes to Net.send ( lib/net/net.dart ), and on to Switchboard.send . Sealed and routed The switchboard ( lib/net/switchboard.dart ) seals the envelope with the key the two installs share, wraps it as a packet, and tries the routes in order. A message isn't allowed to cost money, so the SMS route is passed over and the hub is tried. Through the hub HubCarrier.send ( lib/net/hub_carrier.dart ) hands it to the relay's hub ( relay/lib/hub.dart ), which passes it to the friend's connected devices, or keeps it and says so. Answered, or waited for Passed on, the sender waits a few seconds for the other app's answer and marks the message delivered. Kept, it is marked sent, and the friend's closed app is woken: an Android phone by an empty data text (at most one every ten minutes), an iPhone by a push from relay/lib/pushes.dart . On the other side The packet arrives at Switchboard , which joins its parts, opens it, drops it if it has been seen before, and answers. Friends stores it, and the conversation changes. Joining a call in a space Allowed? Voice.join ( lib/voice/channels.dart ) checks the hub is reachable and the circle's roles allow voice, and leaves any call already on. The microphone RtcMedia ( lib/voice/rtc.dart ) opens it, with noise removal from native/voicefx in the capture path. On Android a foreground service ( CallService.kt ) keeps the call alive with the screen off. Into the room VoiceSession.join ( lib/voice/voice.dart ) joins the space's room on the hub with the name and token made from the space's seed. The hub answers with who is there. An offer to each The newcomer makes a WebRTC connection to each member and says an offer in the room, sealed with the space's key. Each answers, and both sides exchange candidates the same way. Sound, between the members From there the call's sound and picture go between the members' devices. The hub carried the setup and carries none of the call. Pairing a computer The computer makes an offer PhoneLink.beginPairing ( lib/desktop/link/link.dart ) makes a key pair and 16 random bytes and draws them as a QR code. The phone scans it Desk.begin ( Desk.kt ) makes its own key pair. Both ends now work out the same pairing key from the two key pairs and the code's random bytes ( DeskCrypto , in Kotlin and in lib/desktop/link/crypto.dart ). They connect Over the local network where the phone can be found there, otherwise through a ten-minute channel on the relay. Each connection starts with hellos in the clear, then keys of its own, then everything sealed ( LinkSession , DeskSession.kt ). Six digits Both show six digits made from the pairing key. They match only if nobody is in the middle; the person confirms on both. After that The computer's screens call Sms.instance as a phone's do. LinkCalls ( lib/desktop/remote.dart ) turns each call into a sealed request, DeskCalls in DeskSession.kt runs it on the phone, and the answer is kept sealed on the computer for next time. Adding a Marketplace plugin The catalog MarketState ( lib/market/market_state.dart ) reads the relay's catalog and its list of withdrawals. Checked before it is shown For each entry the app checks the reviewer's signature against the keys it ships with ( lib/plugins/pack/review_keys.dart ), fetches the plugin's file, checks its SHA-256, and reads it ( lib/plugins/pack/manifest.dart ). The card is drawn from the checked file, never from what the catalog says of it. What it may do, then Add addListing ( lib/ui/market/market_flows.dart ) shows what the plugin reads and adds, from the same file. Installed InstalledPlugins.installReviewed ( lib/plugins/pack/installed.dart ) checks it once more, keeps the file, and adds it to the registry as a PackPlugin . The list sorts itself again with the plugin's tags and tabs. At every start The approval is checked again and withdrawals applied, so a plugin withdrawn after it was added stops.
