d: Running the app and the relay from source, the tests, the scripts, and how the code is commented.
x: Everything is in one repository, github.com/InfamousVague/ghost-messaging , under the AGPL-3.0. A build from source isn't signed as the releases are, so it installs as a separate app beside the real one. What you need Flutter (stable), which brings Dart. The relay uses the same Dart and nothing else. For Android: the Android SDK and a phone or emulator. For a Mac or iPhone build: Xcode. Node for the scripts in tool/ and the Discord bot; Go only to build the helper programs in sidecar/ . Run it flutter pub get flutter run # on the connected phone, or -d macos / windows / linux flutter build apk --release --target-platform android-arm64 flutter build macos A computer's build starts in lib/desktop/main.dart ; with no phone paired it runs on its own, with an account and no texts. The app talks to the relay at gogho.st unless Settings › Routes is given another. Run the relay cd relay dart pub get # the test package only dart run bin/relay.dart --port 8787 --verbose # ws://127.0.0.1:8787/hub and /relay/ channel dart compile exe bin/relay.dart -o ghost-relay # one file to run on a server Put it behind a web server that holds the certificate and passes /hub , /relay/* , /files* , /market* , /link/* , /word/* and /feedback to it. Then point an app at it: Settings › Routes takes the hub's address. Running your own lists what it reads from its environment. Tests Run What it covers flutter test The app: about 200 files in test/ , by feature. Screen tests draw each screen and compare it with the picture in test/shots ; --update-goldens writes them again. Several start the real relay in the test's own process and send through it. cd relay dart test The relay, part by part. cd android ./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest The Kotlin that needs no phone: the MMS format, the encryption, the link's sealing and session. cd discord npm test The Discord bot and its bridge. go test ./... in a sidecar/ folder That helper program. flutter test tool/net/live_hub_test.dart --dart-define=HUB=wss://…/hub Two made-up installs through a running relay. tool/net has one of these for each of the relay's parts. flutter test integration_test/… -d macos On a real device: the desktop link against a phone, the native recorder and transcripts. Where two languages must agree to the byte (Kotlin and Dart on a seal, the app and the relay on a plugin's checks), both are tested against the same fixed values, kept in test/*_vectors.json . Scripts Script What it does tool/build-docs.mjs Builds these docs from docs-src into site/docs , with the API reference and the Postman collection. --check fails where site/docs isn't what docs-src makes. tool/ghost-api.mjs A command-line client for the app's API . tool/release*.mjs Build, check and publish a release for Android, Mac, Windows and Linux. Each ends by publishing the source. tool/deploy-relay.mjs , deploy-site.mjs , deploy-discord.mjs Put the relay, the site and the Discord bot on a server. tool/build-*sidecar.sh , build-tdlib.sh Build the helper programs and Telegram's library for each platform. tool/phosphor.mjs and the .py files Make the icons, stickers, effects and sounds the app ships with. Keeping the API docs true The API pages and the Postman collection are made, not written: The app's API comes from the app's own registry. After changing lib/api/methods.dart , run UPDATE_API_DOCS=1 flutter test test/api_reference_test.dart , which writes docs-src/api/app-methods.json . Without the variable the same test fails where the file is behind the code. The relay's routes are listed in docs-src/api/relay-routes.mjs . A route added to relay/lib is added there. node tool/build-docs.mjs then draws both references and writes the collection. How the code is commented The source is written to be read. The conventions, so a change fits in: A file opens by saying what it is for and where it sits: a doc comment on its main class, or on library; . Classes, and any method whose name and signature don't say enough, have a line or two on what they are for and what they promise. Comments say why, and what a caller can rely on; they don't repeat the code. Inside a function, a comment sits above a step whose reason isn't plain: a workaround, an order that matters, a detail of a protocol. Plain words. "Chooses a route for each thing sent" rather than "route selection manager". Where a file has a twin in another language ( DeskCrypto.kt and lib/desktop/link/crypto.dart ), each names the other.

d: The two APIs, how each is reached and signed, and a Postman collection of both.
x: Ghost Messaging has two APIs. The app's API controls one running app: its conversations, plugins, other networks and screens. The relay server's API is what every app speaks to the server that carries messages between them. Both are documented in full here, and both are in one Postman collection. The Postman collection ghost-messaging.postman_collection.json (Postman's v2.1 format; Insomnia, Bruno and others read it too). In Postman: Import , then choose the file or paste its address, https://gogho.st/docs/api/ghost-messaging.postman_collection.json . It holds every method of the app's API and every HTTP route of the relay, each with its parameters described and an example body. It is made from the same lists these pages are drawn from, so it matches them. Set its variables before the first call: Variable Starts as What it is app http://127.0.0.1:8765 Where the app serves its API ( Turn it on ). token empty The app's token, from Settings › API › Copy the token . Sent as Authorization: Bearer on every app request. relay https://gogho.st The relay server. Your own, if you run one. filesToken empty A Files space's token, for the Files routes. ghostKey , ghostTime , ghostSig empty The signing headers of a signed relay route (below). Signed routes Some relay routes are signed with an install's private key, over the request's method, path, time and body. Postman can't make that signature by itself, so those requests carry the headers as variables for you to fill from your own code. Signing a request says exactly what is signed. Routes anyone may read work as they are. The hub and the pairing channels are WebSockets with binary frames, which a collection of HTTP requests can't hold. They are written out in The hub and pairing protocols . The app's API Where On the device, http://127.0.0.1:8765 (the port can be changed); on your network too where allowed; from anywhere through the relay, sealed. Who may call Whoever holds the token (HTTP) or the connection string (through the relay). Off until turned on in developer mode. Shape POST /api/ method with the parameters as a JSON object. Answers {"ok": true, "result": …} or {"ok": false, "error": {"code", "message"}} . Reference App API : every method. The relay server's API Where https://gogho.st , or any server running relay/ . Who may call Anyone, for what is public (the Marketplace's catalog). A Files space's routes need its token. Routes that change something are signed with an install's key. Shape Plain HTTP with JSON or raw bytes, for files, the Marketplace and feedback. WebSockets for the hub and pairing. Reference Relay server API (HTTP) and The hub and pairing protocols (WebSocket). What the relay can and can't see The relay is built to carry what it can't read. Packets, rooms' chat, calls' setup, files and account backups are sealed on the device with keys the server never holds. It sees which installs connect, which talk to which, when, and how much. It knows an install by a name made from its public key, and keeps usernames, linked handles and numbers as hashes. Privacy and safety says the same for people who aren't reading the source.

d: Control the app from a script or another program: every method, what it takes and what it answers.
x: Ghost Messaging has an API: every part of the app, from your conversations to its screens, as methods you can call from a script or another program. It's off until you turn it on, and only someone with your token or connection string can use it. Turn it on Developer mode On your phone, tap Settings › About › Version twelve times. Taps more than two seconds apart start the count again, and from the eighth tap a note counts down. Then Settings › Developer and Settings › API appear. Choose how to reach it API On this phone Serve the API Over HTTP, with a token Allow from Wi-Fi Served on the phone's address on your network too Copy the token From anywhere Through the relay Copy the connection string Serve the API : over HTTP on the phone. From a computer by USB: adb forward tcp:8765 tcp:8765 , then call http://localhost:8765 . Allow from Wi-Fi serves it on your network too. Through the relay : from anywhere. The connection string ( ghostapi1:… ) holds the key every call is sealed with; the relay passes calls along without being able to read them. Keep it as you would a password. Call a method Over HTTP, POST /api/ method with the parameters as a JSON body and your token: curl -s http://localhost:8765/api/conversations.list \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer token ' \ -d '{"limit": 5}' Or with the command-line client in the app's repository ( tool/ghost-api.mjs ): node tool/ghost-api.mjs --token token app.info node tool/ghost-api.mjs --remote ghostapi1: secret networks.chats '{"network": "telegram"}' With no method it lists them all; --doc method shows one's documentation. Requests and answers Request What it does GET /api Everything the API says of itself: every method, as JSON ( api.describe ). GET /api/ method One method's documentation. POST /api/ method Calls it. The body is its parameters as a JSON object, or empty. POST /api The same as one object: {"method": "…", "params": {…}, "id": …} . The id comes back with the answer. Every request but GET / needs Authorization: Bearer token . Answers are JSON: {"ok": true, "result": …} {"ok": false, "error": {"code": "bad_params", "message": "\"thread\" is needed: …"}} Code Status Meaning unauthorized 401 The token is missing or wrong. not_found 404 No such method, or what it named isn't there. bad_params 400 A parameter is missing or of the wrong type, or the body isn't a JSON object. Also 405 for anything but GET and POST. failed 500 The method ran and what it asked failed. The message says why. Parameter types are string , int , bool , list and object , and each call is checked against them before it runs. Through the relay The connection string is ghostapi1: and 64 hex digits: a secret of 32 bytes. Both ends make three things from it with HKDF-SHA256 (salt ghost-api v1 ): the pairing channel they meet on (info relay channel , its first 16 bytes), that channel's token ( relay token ), and an AES-256-GCM key ( seal key ). The app holds the channel as its phone end; a client joins as the other ( Pairing channels ). A request is one binary frame: a 12-byte nonce, then {"method", "params", "id"} sealed with the key (additional data ghost-api-v1 , GCM's tag at the end). The answer comes back the same way. The relay passes the frames and can't open them. The app must be running to answer. tool/ghost-api.mjs is a client of about 150 lines to read or copy from. The methods Settings › API › Methods lists the same, with a place to try each. Those marked changes things send, delete or change something, and ask before running there. d: The relay server's HTTP routes: files, the Marketplace, feedback and the rest.
x:
The relay is mostly two WebSockets, the hub and the pairing relay. Beside them it answers a small set of plain HTTP routes: a circle's sealed files, the plugin Marketplace, feedback, and the pages that link a handle. This page lists every one. The public relay is at https://gogho.st . Anyone can run their own from the source: dart run relay/bin/relay.dart --port 8787 . The WebSocket protocols are on The hub and pairing protocols , and a Postman collection of these routes is on API overview and Postman . Conventions No CORS. The relay sets no Access-Control-* header and has no OPTIONS handling. These routes are for the app and for scripts, not for a page in a browser on another site. No match is not an error. A request that fits no route, whatever its method, answers 200 with the plain text Ghost Messaging relay . There is no separate health route: this is it. JSON answers are application/json; charset=utf-8 . Request bodies are read as UTF-8 JSON or raw bytes; no Content-Type is looked at. Hex is lowercase. Ids and hashes in paths must match their shape exactly, or the route does not exist. Times are whole milliseconds since 1970, as decimal digits. Per-address limits go by the first value of X-Forwarded-For , or the connection's address where there is none. Each module says no in its own shape: Module A refusal Notes Files {"err": "No such space."} A sentence. A few carry more: have , done , seq . Feedback {"error": "Feedback is sent with POST."} A sentence, under error , not err . Marketplace {"ok": false, "error": "not_found", "message": "There's nothing here by that name."} error is a fixed code; message is for people. Every success carries "ok": true . Outside the modules, a path whose percent-escapes are not UTF-8 answers 400 with no body, and an error nothing else caught answers 500 with no body. Signing a request Writes to Files, feedback, and most of the Marketplace are signed with the install's own key, the same one the hub knows it by. No account or password is involved. Thing Format Key P-256 (secp256r1). The public key is 33 bytes compressed: 02 or 03 , then x. In a header it is standard base64 with padding, 44 characters. Signature ECDSA over the SHA-256 of the signed string. 64 bytes: r (32, big-endian) then s (32). Not DER. Standard base64, 88 characters. Id The first 16 bytes of the SHA-256 of the 33 key bytes, as 32 lowercase hex digits. This is who the relay says wrote something. Body hash SHA-256 of the body's bytes, 64 lowercase hex digits. For an empty body: e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855 . All three modules take the same three headers and sign five lines joined by a line feed ( 
 ), as UTF-8, with no line feed after the last. Only the first line and a few rules differ. x-ghost-key: base64 of the 33-byte public key x-ghost-time: milliseconds since 1970 x-ghost-sig: base64 of the 64-byte signature The relay remembers what each key signed, so the same request sent twice is refused the second time. To try again, sign again with a new time. Files Every Files route but GET /files also carries the space's token: Authorization: Ghost token , 64 lowercase hex digits. Reads need only the token. Writes need the token and the signature. ghost-files v1 METHOD path and query, as sent time body sha256 hex The third line is the whole request target, query included: /files/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef/log?after=7 . The time may be up to 10 minutes from the relay's clock, either way. Where the body is not read ( DELETE /files/{space} , POST …/done ), sign the empty body's hash. For a blob's piece sent with x-ghost-body-sha256 , the last line is that header's value, and the signature is checked before the body is read. Any failure answers 401 {"err": "Bad signature."} . Feedback ghost-feedback v1 POST /feedback time body sha256 hex The third line is the path alone, with no query. The time may be up to 5 minutes from the relay's clock. Marketplace ghost-market v1 METHOD path time body sha256 hex The third line is the path alone. A signed request with any query string is refused. The time may be up to 5 minutes from the relay's clock. A POST must say its body up front, in two more headers: x-ghost-body-sha256 (64 lowercase hex digits; the last signed line) and x-ghost-body-length (the length in bytes, equal to Content-Length ). A chunked body is refused. A GET or DELETE must send neither of those headers and no body, and signs the empty body's hash. A missing header answers 401 unsigned . A bad key, time or signature, or a repeat, answers 401 bad_signature . A broken shape (a query, a header sent twice, a length that does not match) answers 400 bad_request . A signed GET /market/mine looks like this: GET /market/mine HTTP/1.1 Host: gogho.st x-ghost-key: AqGyw9Tl9gcYKTpLXG1+j5ChssPU5fYHGCk6S1xtfo+Q x-ghost-time: 1795000000000 x-ghost-sig: 88 base64 characters and its signature is over these bytes: ghost-market v1 GET /market/mine 1795000000000 e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855 Signatures inside Marketplace bodies Review's decisions are signed a second time, by the reviewer's key, so that the apps can check them without trusting the relay. Each is the same kind of signature over lines joined by

When someone links a Discord, Telegram or X handle, the app asks the hub for a sign-in address and opens it. The address holds a state made for that install, good for 10 minutes and for one sign-in. The relay checks the sign-in with the network, links the handle, and tells the install over the hub. A network whose keys are not set on the server is off, and its page says the link is no good. This one route is how the site's join page looks a word up. GET /word/{h} The sealed invite link kept under a word's hash. The word itself is never sent. The relay can't read either: names, keys and contents are sealed by the apps. It sees the space's id, each blob's size, when things were written, and the id of the install that wrote them. d: What an app says to the relay server over a WebSocket: signing in, packets, presence, rooms and the directory.
x: The relay server speaks two WebSocket protocols. The hub is where installs find each other: any address ending in /hub , so wss://gogho.st/hub . A pairing channel joins one phone to one of its computers: an address ending in 32 hex digits, wss://gogho.st/relay/ channel . Both pass sealed bytes the server can't read. Its plain HTTP routes are in the relay's HTTP routes , and how the app uses all of this is in Routes . On both, a text frame is one JSON object and a binary frame is a sealed packet. The server pings each socket every 30 seconds. The code is relay/lib/hub.dart and relay/lib/relay.dart ; the app's side of the hub is lib/net/hub_carrier.dart . Who an install is An install is a P-256 (secp256r1) key pair made on the device. The hub knows it by a name made from the public key. There is no account to make first: anyone with a key can sign in. Thing What it is Public key 33 bytes, compressed: 02 or 03 , then x. Sent as base64 in the sign-in, whois and acct-put ; as 66 lowercase hex digits for a read-only room's owner . Name (id) The first 16 bytes of SHA-256 of those 33 bytes, as 32 lowercase hex digits. In binary frames it is the 16 raw bytes. Signature ECDSA over SHA-256 of the message, as 64 raw bytes: r, then s, big-endian. Not DER. Sent as base64 in the sign-in and in bind ; as 128 lowercase hex digits in a read-only room's grants. Account address A Ghost account is a second key, secp256k1, known by an Ethereum-style address: 0x and 40 hex digits. Only the account messages use it. All hex the server reads is lowercase. Signing in to the hub Open a WebSocket to wss://gogho.st/hub . With 20,000 sockets open already, the upgrade is refused with HTTP 503 . The hub speaks first, with a number made for this connection (32 random bytes, as 64 hex digits): {"hello": " 64 hex ", "peek": true, "react": true} peek says this hub knows the look-only sign-in below. react says it takes reaction packets . Within 10 seconds, answer with one text frame: {"id": " 32 hex ", "key": " base64, 33 bytes ", "sig": " base64, 64 bytes ", "device": "desk-1"} The hub answers, then hands over what it held for you as binary frames: {"ok": true, "held": 3} Field What it holds id Your name. It must be the one made from key . key Your public key, base64. sig Your signature, base64, over the 13 bytes of ghost-hub v1 (with its space) followed by the 32 raw bytes of the hub's number: the hex decoded, not the hex text. device Optional. Which of your devices this is, 64 characters at most. Left out, too long or not a string, it counts as the empty string. peek Optional. true makes this a look only. One name can be signed in from 8 devices at once. A new connection with the same device takes the older one's place, and a ninth device takes the place of the one connected longest. The connection that lost its place is closed with 4409 . A look With "peek": true the hub says how much is waiting and closes the socket with 1000 ( looked ). Nothing is handed over or removed, and no other connection of yours is replaced. A closed app uses it to see whether it should wake. {"ok": true, "held": 3, "peek": true, "here": false} here says whether any device of this name is connected now.
